stem: Which activity is query monitoring in an AI system?

options.text: Measuring how long the model takes to answer each separate request
Inspecting incoming prompts for injection and private data
Comparing replies with a labeled set of correct answers
Counting the tokens that each team uses every month

explanation: Query monitoring watches what users send in: injection attempts, restricted topics, and sensitive values. Latency tracking is performance monitoring, comparing replies with a labeled set is an accuracy audit, and token counts by team are cost monitoring.

stem: What does response monitoring look for?

options.text: Sensitive data, unsafe content, or unsupported claims in replies
Unusual request volume arriving from a single client key overnight
Changes made to the access rights of model administrators
Growth in the storage used by retained conversation history

explanation: Response monitoring inspects what the model sends back so that leaks, harmful text, and fabricated claims can be flagged. Request volume is rate monitoring, access rights belong to an access audit, and storage growth is a cost signal.

stem: After a complaint, a review finds that a support assistant sent one customer another customer's home address from a retrieved record. Which monitoring control would have caught it before the customer saw it?

options.text: Rate monitoring on the support team's service account
Cost alerts on monthly token spend for the assistant
Response monitoring that scans replies for personal data
Query monitoring that blocks prompts containing profanity

explanation: Response monitoring scans model output for personal data patterns and catches a leak at the point it would be delivered. Rate monitoring and cost alerts do not read content, and a profanity filter on the prompt side cannot see what the model returns.

stem: Over ten minutes, one account sends forty prompts that repeat the same request with small wording changes, each aimed at getting the assistant to ignore its rules. What does query monitoring conclude?

options.text: The account is load testing the gateway capacity for a release
The account quota is set too low for normal use
The reply cache needs a longer expiry for repeated questions
The account is probing for a guardrail bypass

explanation: Repeated rewording against the same restricted goal is the pattern of someone probing for a bypass, so an alert and a review of the account are warranted. Load testing would not vary the wording to dodge rules, a low quota would not explain the content, and caching has nothing to do with intent.

stem: A customer disputes what the assistant told them last month. The log must show who asked and which model answered, yet the company does not want to store customer conversations. Which log entry design fits?

options.text: Source network only, with no user or model detail
Training data lineage, tuning logs, and serial numbers
Account, model version, timestamp, and a hash of the exchange
Full reply text and the complete conversation transcript

explanation: Naming the account, model version, and time attributes the exchange, and a hash lets investigators later verify any retained copy without storing the text. A network address alone cannot attribute activity, lineage describes the model rather than the interaction, and full transcripts keep the sensitive content the company wants to avoid.

stem: The gateway blocks a prompt, and a minute later the same user session triggers a refund tool call. Analysts see the two events in separate tools and cannot link them. What fixes this?

options.text: Send both logs to the SIEM with a shared trace tag
Raise the log verbosity on the gateway alone for a week
Rotate both log files more often during the working day
Give analysts login rights on the tool host machine

explanation: Central collection with a correlating tag lets one query show the blocked prompt and the tool call together. Extra verbosity on one source and faster rotation leave the logs separate, and host logins make analysts search by hand while widening access.

stem: A review of the prompt log store finds full payment card numbers that users pasted into chat. The team still wants the logs for debugging. Which action best addresses this?

options.text: Move the log files to a faster storage tier
Mask card numbers before entries are written
Add a banner asking users not to share card numbers
Compress the logs so the numbers are harder to read

explanation: Sanitizing at write time keeps the debugging value of the log while the card numbers never land in storage. A faster tier changes nothing about content, a banner relies on user behavior, and compression is trivially reversed.

stem: What is log sanitization?

options.text: Deleting every log older than the retention period
Checking that timestamps match across all servers
Compressing logs to reduce the storage space they take
Masking sensitive values before storing entries

explanation: Sanitization removes or masks sensitive values such as personal data or secrets so they are not kept in the log. Deleting old logs is retention, aligning clocks is time synchronization, and compression is storage management.

stem: All forty developers on a team can open the production prompt logs, which sometimes hold customer details. Which log-protection change fits best?

options.text: Email a weekly log summary to the developer team
Copy the logs to each laptop for faster searching
Limit read access to named roles and log who opens them
Move the logs into the application source repository

explanation: Role-limited access with an access record applies least privilege and leaves an audit trail for the logs themselves. Mailing summaries and copying to laptops spread the data further, and a source repository is readable by even more people.

stem: An intruder with administrator rights on the application server deletes the log lines that record their session. Which design best protects the evidence?

options.text: Keep logs in a folder only the application owner can change
Rotate the local logs every hour
Keep a second copy on the same server in another folder
Stream entries to write-once storage under separate credentials

explanation: Logs shipped off the host to write-once storage with separate credentials cannot be erased by someone who controls the server. A folder permission, rotation, or a second copy on the same machine all fall to the same administrator.

stem: A prompt log store keeps every conversation indefinitely, although the privacy notice promises deletion after a fixed period. Which control closes the gap?

options.text: A retention schedule that expires entries on the stated timeline
A larger archive disk so the logs never run out of room for new entries
A weekly report that counts how many logs exist in the archive
Encryption of the logs with a stronger cipher

explanation: An automated retention rule makes actual practice match the promise. More disk space enlarges the problem, a count report only describes it, and stronger encryption protects the data without ending its retention.

stem: What does a response confidence level indicate?

options.text: How quickly the model produced the reply for a user
How sure the system is that its answer is right
How many users rated the reply as helpful or not
How much it cost to generate the reply

explanation: A confidence level is an estimate of how likely an answer is to be right, which can drive review decisions. Speed is latency, ratings are user feedback, and generation cost is a spend metric.

stem: An internal assistant attaches a confidence score to every answer, and answers scoring under 0.4 are becoming a larger share of traffic. Which use of the score best protects users?

options.text: Hide the score so that users are not confused by it
Retrain the model each time a low score appears in traffic
Delete low-scoring answers from the logs
Route weak answers to a person or add a warning

explanation: Acting on a low score, through human review or a visible warning, keeps users from relying on shaky answers. Hiding the score removes the signal, retraining on every instance is impractical, and deleting log entries destroys evidence needed for the trend.

stem: A model answers a legal question with a confidence score of 0.97 but cites a court case that does not exist. What does this show?

options.text: The score is dependable and the citation lookup must have failed
The score measures only how fast the reply was generated
A high score can still be wrong, so check claims against sources
The prompt was too short to produce a usable score

explanation: A fluent model can be confident and wrong, so the score is one signal and must be paired with grounding checks and sampling. The case does not exist, so a failed citation lookup cannot be the cause. The score is not a speed measure, and prompt length does not explain a fabricated case.

stem: What does rate monitoring track?

options.text: The volume of requests each client sends over time
The accuracy of answers measured against a labeled test set
The number of administrators with access to the model
The storage used by the retained conversation history of every user

explanation: Rate monitoring measures how many requests arrive, per client and per period, so spikes and abuse stand out. The other options describe an accuracy audit, an access audit, and a storage cost metric.

stem: On a quiet Sunday, a reporting key that usually makes 15 requests an hour jumps to 700 an hour, all from a network never seen before. What is the best response?

options.text: Raise the key limit so legitimate traffic is not blocked
Alert, suspend or rotate the key, and review its activity
Wait for the monthly invoice to confirm that the spike is real
Delete the logs for that period to save space

explanation: A sharp departure from a normal rate on a new network suggests a leaked key or runaway job, so contain it and investigate. Raising the limit lets the abuse continue, waiting for the invoice delays containment, and deleting logs destroys the evidence.

stem: An attacker sends one request every 40 seconds, far under the gateway limit, with prompts that methodically cover a topic area over several weeks. Which monitoring is most likely to catch this?

options.text: Per-minute request caps enforced at the gateway edge
Alerts on the response latency of single requests
Daily token totals for the whole company across every team
Multi-day client baselines with input variety checks

explanation: A slow, systematic sweep stays beneath short-window limits, so detection needs long-horizon per-client baselines and content patterns. Per-minute caps never trigger, single-request latency looks normal, and company-wide totals hide one client.

stem: An assistant's monthly bill doubles after a developer adds twelve pages of policy text to every request. Which cost driver should the team monitor?

options.text: Output tokens per generated reply, split by feature
Stored embeddings per vector index, split by feature
Input tokens per prompt, split by feature
GPU hours per tuning job

explanation: The added text enlarges every prompt, so tracking input tokens per prompt by feature exposes the change. Output tokens, stored embeddings, and tuning hours did not change when the prompt template grew.

stem: A chat product keeps every conversation and its embeddings for audit, and storage charges climb each month. What should the team monitor?

options.text: Growth in kept data by type, with retention rules
Input tokens per prompt on the busiest day of the month
Peak requests per second at the gateway during the day
Processing time of each generated reply

explanation: Storage cost follows how much data is kept and for how long, so growth by data type and lifecycle rules are the levers. Prompt size, request peaks, and latency belong to other cost or performance categories.

stem: Replies from a summarizer average 1,800 tokens when users need about 300, and output tokens are priced higher than input tokens. Which control cuts this cost?

options.text: Move the summarizer to a larger instance size for the model
Cache the incoming prompts at the gateway
Raise the per-user request limit
Set a maximum length and ask the model to be brief

explanation: Response cost scales with generated tokens, so bounding length attacks it directly. A larger instance raises processing spend, prompt caching affects input rather than output, and a higher limit invites more usage.

stem: Fine-tuning jobs start at random times, and many leave GPUs idle while waiting for data. Which measure targets this processing cost?

options.text: Shorten the system prompt used by the production assistant
Track compute utilization and schedule training runs
Mask sensitive values in the application logs
Archive old conversations to cold storage

explanation: Processing spend is driven by compute time, so utilization tracking and scheduling reduce waste. System prompt length affects input cost, log masking is sanitization, and cold storage changes the storage bill.

stem: A nightly batch job that summarizes a document archive is misconfigured and resubmits the whole archive every ten minutes, using a month of budget by morning. Which control would have stopped the spending soonest?

options.text: An automatic spend cap and a limit on repeat runs
A weekly cost review held by the finance team
A longer retention period for the job logs
A larger context window for the summarizer

explanation: Automated limits react in minutes: a spend cap that suspends the job and a limit on repeated runs break a resubmission storm quickly. A weekly review comes too late, longer retention records the storm without stopping it, and a larger context window does nothing to curb repeats.

stem: A dashboard alerts on blocked prompts all day. Once a quarter, reviewers sample outputs against a written checklist and file a report. What is the quarterly activity?

options.text: Monitoring, since it watches the live system continuously
Sanitization, since it masks sensitive values in logs
Auditing, since it is a scheduled criteria-based review
Rate limiting, since it caps requests per client

explanation: A scheduled, deeper review against stated criteria with a written report is an audit, while the all-day dashboard is monitoring. Sanitization masks values in logs and rate limiting caps client volume, and neither involves sampling outputs for review.

stem: To measure hallucination in a document-answering assistant, auditors sample replies. What do they compare each reply against?

options.text: The confidence score the model gave to the reply
The satisfaction rating from the user
The volume of data used in training
The source documents retrieved for the response

explanation: A hallucination is a claim the sources do not support, so each sampled claim is checked against the retrieved material. A confidence score can be high on fabricated text, satisfaction reflects tone more than truth, and training volume says nothing about one reply.

stem: An auditor needs to know whether an incident-triage model has become less accurate since its last release. Which evidence is best?

options.text: The number of user complaints received during this week
Test-set results compared with the previous release
The average reply length measured for the new release
Gateway latency measured across both releases in use

explanation: Accuracy is measured against known correct labels, and comparing releases on the same set isolates the change. Complaints are noisy and incomplete, reply length and latency are unrelated to correctness.

stem: An audit of a resume-ranking assistant finds that equally qualified candidates from one group are ranked lower. Which audit check surfaced this?

options.text: Comparing token usage across the two candidate groups
Measuring the latency of each ranking request
Comparing outcomes across groups for like inputs
Verifying that the model endpoint uses TLS

explanation: Fairness auditing holds qualifications constant and compares results between groups. Token usage, latency, and transport encryption can all look normal while the ranking is skewed.

stem: An access audit lists seven accounts with read rights on the prompt logs. Two belong to staff who changed teams a year ago, and one is a shared login. What is the right finding and fix?

options.text: Access is stale and shared; remove old rights and use named accounts
Accounts are fine because every holder once had a business need
Access is too narrow; grant the logs to the whole department
Only the shared login matters because it is the easiest to guess

explanation: Stale rights break least privilege and a shared login destroys accountability, so both should be corrected. Past need does not justify current access, widening access adds risk, and the two stale accounts are also findings.

stem: An auditor must confirm that the content filter was switched on during an incident last spring. Which record shows this?

options.text: A dashboard showing today's average response latency
A cost report grouped by team and month
A guardrail test report from the original launch
Dated change history for its moderation settings

explanation: Dated change records show what the filter configuration was on a given day, which is the traceability an audit needs. A latency dashboard and a cost report say nothing about the filter, and a launch-time test shows only that it worked then.

stem: A fairness audit finds that a loan assistant approves 60% of applications from group one and 45% from group two, with similar qualifications. What is group two's approval rate divided by group one's?

options.text: About 0.25
About 0.75
About 1.33
About 15

explanation: Dividing group two's approval rate of 45 by group one's of 60 gives 0.75, a disparity the audit should investigate and document. Neither 0.25 nor 15 is the quotient of these rates, and 1.33 inverts the division.

stem: An audit finds that an assistant calculates refund amounts incorrectly, and the team ships a fix. What should the auditor do before closing the finding?

options.text: Re-run the failed test cases and record the result
Close it once the developer says it is fixed
Remove the original finding to keep the report short and tidy
Wait for the next annual audit to see if it recurs

explanation: A finding is closed on verified evidence, so the failed cases are tested again and the outcome is recorded. A verbal assurance is unverified, deleting findings removes the audit trail, and waiting a year leaves the defect unconfirmed.

stem: Refusals from an internal coding assistant doubled over a weekend, and nobody noticed until Wednesday. Which addition would have flagged the change earlier?

options.text: A longer retention period for the request logs on the gateway
A monthly report that lists the model builds available to staff
An alert on the share of declines against its rolling baseline
A larger log disk on the gateway host

explanation: An alert comparing the share of declines with its recent baseline raises the shift within minutes instead of days. More retention, a monthly report, and extra disk space all keep or list data without watching it for change.

stem: Which TWO fields belong in each AI request log entry at a minimum?

options.text: Full response text for every request
Caller identity for the account or service
The caller's home address
Model version that produced the reply
The source code of the model
The raw encryption keys used by the service

explanation: Caller identity and model version attribute each request to a person or service and a specific model, which is the minimum for tracing. Full response text and home addresses add sensitive data the log does not need, and source code and keys must never be written to a log.

stem: Which THREE measures protect AI logs that contain prompts?

options.text: Encrypt the logs both at rest and in transit
Keep every log until someone asks to delete it
Restrict read access to a few named roles
Give all engineers read access for debugging
Send a copy to separate write-once storage
Store logs on the web server for fast access

explanation: Encryption, role-limited access, and a protected off-host copy keep logs confidential and tamper resistant. Open-ended retention, broad read access, and web-server storage each increase exposure.

stem: Which TWO patterns in monitored queries suggest someone is trying to extract a model's behavior?

options.text: Occasional questions from staff about the holiday calendar
Short greetings sent from a front-desk kiosk screen
Many systematic variations of one topic from one account
One long prompt pasted by a newly hired employee
Scripted runs of near-identical inputs at steady intervals
Requests that match a user's usual working hours and topics

explanation: Extraction looks like methodical, machine-paced coverage of an input space by one source. Calendar questions, greetings, one long prompt, and ordinary working patterns are normal use.

stem: Which TWO factors drive the processing cost of an AI service?

options.text: GPU hours consumed by inference and tuning jobs
The size of the model chosen for each request
Gigabytes of embeddings kept in the vector index
Months of conversation history kept for audit
The length of the log retention schedule
The number of users with read access to logs

explanation: Compute time and the size of the model doing the work set processing spend. Stored embeddings and kept history are storage costs, and retention length and the number of log readers do not change the compute bill.

stem: Which TWO responses fit answers that fall below a set confidence threshold?

options.text: Send the answer faster to avoid user frustration
Remove the answer from the logs
Retrain the model after every low score
Route the answer to a human reviewer
Hide the score from the interface
Show a visible caveat or ask a clarifying question

explanation: Low confidence is a cue for oversight or a user-facing warning. Speeding delivery ignores the risk, removing logs loses evidence, per-answer retraining is impractical, and hiding the score discards the signal.

stem: Which THREE belong in an audit of an assistant for hallucinations?

options.text: Sample replies and check their claims against sources
Track the share of unsupported claims across releases
Include questions the sources cannot answer
Measure how long each page takes to load for users
Count total user logins across the staff accounts
Compare the monthly cloud bill for each team and service

explanation: Source checks, a trend of the unsupported-claim rate, and questions the sources cannot answer (to see whether it admits uncertainty) reveal fabrication. Page speed, logins, and billing are unrelated to whether answers are true.

stem: Which TWO checks belong in an access audit of an AI platform?

options.text: Measure whether replies show demographic bias
Compare labeled test-set scores between releases
Total the monthly token spend by team
Review accounts with rights to models, data, and logs
Verify that replies cite their sources
Confirm that dormant and shared accounts are removed

explanation: An access audit asks who can reach models, data, and logs, and whether those rights are still justified. Bias, test-set scores, spend, and citations belong to fairness, accuracy, cost, and hallucination reviews.

stem: The gateway rate report compares each client's normal request rate with the last ten minutes. Use it to answer each question.

fields.label: Client with the largest rise over its own baseline

options.text: hr-bot
partner-api
sales-copilot
docs-search

fields.label: That client's observed rate as a multiple of its baseline

options.text: 4 times
8 times
20 times
500 times

fields.label: Total observed requests per minute across all clients
Best first response for that client, whose traffic was not announced

options.text: Treat it as normal variation and keep current limits
Raise its limit to match the new observed rate
Delete its baseline and start over from fresh data
Suspend or rotate its key and review its activity

explanation: The partner-api client shows the largest jump: 500 against a baseline of 25. A rate monitor compares each client with its own history, so the sharpest multiple stands out even when another client sends more in absolute terms.

partExplanations.spike: sales-copilot is 4 times baseline, but partner-api is 500 / 25, far higher; hr-bot and docs-search are near or below baseline.
partExplanations.action: A 20-fold jump from a small client suggests a leaked key or runaway job, so contain and investigate before raising limits.

stem: Use the monthly usage table and the stated prices to answer each cost question.

payload.caption: Monthly AI usage by feature. Prices: $3 per million prompt tokens, $12 per million response tokens, $0.10 per gigabyte stored, $4 per GPU hour.

fields.label: Feature with the highest prompt cost

options.text: Helpdesk
Search
Summarizer

fields.label: Feature whose largest cost category is response tokens

options.text: Helpdesk
Search
Summarizer

fields.label: Total monthly cost across all three features
Cost category with the largest total

options.text: Storage
Processing
Response tokens
Prompt tokens

explanation: Price each category per feature, then total. Prompt tokens are the largest category at $540, ahead of response tokens at $480, processing at $180, and storage at $130.

partExplanations.promptTop: Search uses 120 million prompt tokens at $3, which is $360, more than Helpdesk ($120) or Summarizer ($60).
partExplanations.respTop: Summarizer response cost is 25 x $12 = $300 of its $390 total; the other features lead elsewhere.
partExplanations.topCat: Prompt $540, response $480, processing $180, storage $130, so prompt tokens lead.

stem: An analyst is reviewing the AI gateway log after a burst of blocked requests. Read the output, then complete each step.

output: 10:14:09 client=svc-bravo model=assist-2 status=blocked rule=r14 note="ignore the previous instructions"
10:14:11 client=svc-bravo model=assist-2 status=blocked rule=r14 note="ignore the previous instructions"
10:14:18 client=svc-bravo model=assist-2 status=blocked rule=r14 note="ignore the previous instructions"
10:14:21 client=svc-bravo model=assist-2 status=blocked rule=r14 note="ignore the previous instructions"
# grep pattern file prints matching lines; grep -c pattern file prints how many lines match

steps.label: Type a command that shows every line in gateway.log containing status=blocked
Type a command that prints how many lines in gateway.log mention client=svc-bravo
Which risk does the repeated note from svc-bravo point to?

options.text: Training data poisoning
Prompt injection attempts
Model theft by extraction
Hallucination in replies
Raise the gateway limits for svc-bravo to stop the blocks
Turn off the blocking rule to cut down the noise in logs
Suspend the svc-bravo key and review its prompts
Clear gateway.log so the next review starts from clean

explanation: The log shows one client repeatedly blocked for an override phrase. grep filters the lines, grep -c counts them, and the pattern is prompt injection probing that calls for containing the key and reviewing the source.

partExplanations.blocked: grep status=blocked gateway.log prints only the blocked lines.
partExplanations.count: grep -c counts the lines that match client=svc-bravo.
partExplanations.risk: Repeated attempts to override instructions are prompt injection attempts, not poisoning, theft, or hallucination.
partExplanations.act: Suspending the key and reviewing the source contains the activity; raising limits, disabling the rule, or clearing the log helps the abuser or destroys evidence.

stem: The chat application's prompt log holds pasted card numbers and is readable by everyone on the host. Read the output, then complete each step.

output: 09:02:11 user=u1842 prompt="my card is 4111111111111111 and it was declined"
# logscrub --mask card --in infile --out outfile   masks card numbers into a new file
# chmod mode file   mode is three digits for owner, group, others (4 read, 2 write, 1 run)

steps.label: Type the command that masks card numbers in prompts.log and writes the result to prompts.clean.log
Type a command that gives prompts.clean.log owner read and write, group read only, and others no access
What should happen to the original prompts.log once the clean copy is verified and no legal hold applies?

options.text: Keep it beside the clean copy as a backup for the team
Securely delete it so no copy keeps the data
Email it to the compliance team for their records
Rename it prompts.old and leave it in the same folder

steps.label: Where should the clean copy go for long-term review?

options.text: A SIEM index with role-restricted read access
A shared drive open to the whole company
A public bucket so vendors can read it
Each developer's laptop

explanation: Sanitization masks the card numbers into a new file, protection tightens the file mode, and the unsanitized original is removed so the sensitive values are not kept anywhere. The clean copy goes to a restricted store.

partExplanations.scrub: logscrub with --mask card, an input file and an output file writes a masked copy.
partExplanations.perm: Mode 640 gives owner read and write (6), group read (4), and others nothing (0).
partExplanations.orig: Leaving, mailing, or renaming the original keeps card numbers in storage; secure deletion removes them.
partExplanations.ship: A SIEM index with role-restricted access protects the log; open shares, public buckets, and laptops expose it.

stem: An AI chat service sends user traffic through a gateway to a model host and writes events through a log pipeline to a log store. Select every component that performs prompt or response monitoring, log sanitization, or log protection (not cost tracking).

nodes.text: Billing exporter: totals spend per team
Model host: runs inference on GPU nodes
Log store: encrypted, read access by role

spots.name: Billing exporter: totals spend per team
Model host: runs inference on GPU nodes
Log store: encrypted, read access by role

explanation: Inspection of prompts and replies happens at the gateway, masking happens in the log pipeline before storage, and protection happens at the log store through encryption and role-based access. The billing exporter and the model host do none of these jobs.

partExplanations.billing: Totalling spend is cost monitoring, not prompt monitoring, sanitization, or log protection.
partExplanations.mask: Masking before write is log sanitization.
partExplanations.host: The model host serves inference; it does not monitor or protect logs.
partExplanations.vault: Encryption and role-limited reads are log protection.

stem: Put the steps of an audit for AI quality and compliance in the order they are carried out.

steps.text: Rate each failed check by severity and write up the evidence
Define the audit scope, systems, and pass criteria
Re-test the fixed items and close findings with proof
Collect output samples, logs, and access lists
Assign remediation owners and due dates
Test the samples against the criteria for hallucination, accuracy, and bias

explanation: An audit moves from scope to evidence to testing, then records findings, assigns fixes, and verifies them before closure.

partExplanations.0: Scope and criteria come first so the rest of the work is measured against something.
partExplanations.1: Evidence is gathered once the scope is known.
partExplanations.2: The samples are tested against the criteria.
partExplanations.3: Findings are recorded with severity and evidence after testing.
partExplanations.4: Owners and dates turn findings into remediation work.
partExplanations.5: Re-testing confirms the fixes before findings are closed.

stem: An auditor logged six findings on a human resources assistant. Sort each finding into the audit category it belongs to.

items.text: The assistant cited a policy section that does not exist in the handbook
On factual questions, only 81% of answers matched the reference set, down from 92% last quarter
Applicants from one postal region are declined twice as often as equally qualified applicants elsewhere
Replies to the same question use warmer wording for some first names than others
Fourteen former contractors still hold read rights to the prompt logs
Five engineers query the model with one shared administrator login

explanation: Fabricated references are hallucination, a score against known answers is accuracy, unequal treatment of groups is bias and fairness, and who can reach the system is access.

partExplanations.i1: A citation to something that does not exist is a fabricated claim, which is hallucination.
partExplanations.i2: A match rate against a reference set measures accuracy.
partExplanations.i3: Different outcomes for equally qualified people by region is a fairness finding.
partExplanations.i4: Different treatment by first name is a bias finding.
partExplanations.i5: Stale rights to sensitive logs are an access finding.
partExplanations.i6: A shared administrator login is an access finding because it removes accountability.
